## Early-Stage Non-Conventional Hardware Accelerator Discovery via Optimization Methods and Compiler Analysis

Abstract

In the post-Moore era, where we witness the diminishing returns of traditional

transistor scaling, a pivotal transition in accelerator design methodologies has been

necessitated to continually enhance power, performance, and area (PPA) characteris-

tics. To this end, High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools have emerged as a prominent so-

lution, effectively translating high-level programs into specific Register-Transfer Level

(RTL) implementations. These tools offer a multitude of implementation pathways,

thereby accommodating the escalating demand for PPA optimization.

Concurrently, the development of advanced design space exploration (DSE) utilities

has significantly refined the simulation of hardware-software co-designed systems, de-

livering high-fidelity point solutions without the complexity of HLS toolchains or their

accompanying simulators. However, these late-stage DSE tools are not without their

shortcomings; they impose a substantial manual burden on the developer to dissect

the application. This task demands a nuanced understanding of computational gran-

ularity, partitioning overheads, and opportunities for reusing circuitry—insights not

readily furnished by existing tools.

The prevailing trajectory in this field is to escalate the abstraction level at which

designers can evaluate system configurations, thereby reducing reliance on HLS and

late-stage DSE tools and enhancing automation. At the research frontier, we probe

iii

whether it is possible to derive insights into potential accelerator designs, hardware-

software partitioning, and circuit reuse directly from the source code of applications

coded in high-level languages like C++, supplemented by profiling data.

In this thesis, we identify the limitations and opportunities available at this level

of abstraction. We discover coarse-grained patterns that help design area and energy-

eﬀicient accelerators and partitioning schemes aware of the function call-graph hierar-

chies. We identify sequence alignment techniques, mixed integer linear programming,

and machine learning for systems as great methods to assist the next generation of

system-design tools. We observe that related work does not analyze the impact of

hardware models in the accelerator selection or pattern detection problems. Our

analysis in these areas allows us to create tools better at selecting energy, area, and

latency-eﬀicient accelerators. Our approach allows extracting this valuable informa-

tion in the earliest design stages with low error, with close-to-global optimum designs.

## Introduction

1.1 Motivation

The end of Moore’s law creates a demand for novel ways to meet the speed, cost,

and energy requirements in novel application domains as well as for established ap-

plication domains. One of the key layers to achieve progress in this area is through

hardware/software co-design and relying on hardware accelerators to deliver orders of

1


<!-- Page 17 -->


magnitude of PPA improvements.

Accelerators are implemented using limited area budgets, allowing few applications

to benefit from acceleration. Moreover, designers rely on their intuitions of where the

bottlenecks are in the applications they accelerate. They rely on software profiling

tools that are helpful for CPU optimizations but very limited for designing future

systems that contain CPUs and accelerators. Software profiling-driven acceleration of

program regions is agnostic of the CPU-accelerator connection latency and bandwidth

requirements as well as the area cost of the accelerated region. Consequently, early in

the SoC design stages, designers partition their applications sub-optimally and start

time-consuming iterative synthesis and accelerator optimization flows, which deliver

far-from-optimal system-wide PPA results. Throughout this dissertation, we label

early-stage design space exploration as EDSE.

Previous solutions have attempted to create application analysis tools that provide

early-stage system design information, but they lack in three important dimensions.

• A) Co-design of the hardware models for PPA and the optimization models.

Since the application is not in an HLS-friendly format or partitioned in the

early stages, the early-stage design tools must rely on models for partitioning

the application and effective area reuse insights. Those related work tools do

not analyze the effect of relying on models for the PPA rather than completely

accurate information. In this thesis, we show that the impact on the end-to-

end EDSE reports and their effectiveness in achieving optimal partitioning is

severely affected by this lack of model study.

• B) Early-DSE that uses significant late-stage information. Most tools that at-

tempt EDSE rely on significant late-stage design information, such as reports

2


<!-- Page 18 -->


from HLS tools or even the premature specification of highly optimized acceler-

ator implementation, resulting in suboptimal system design choices and defeat-

ing the purpose of early-stage design space exploration.

• C) Lack of control and data-flow graph (CDFG) pattern detection and granu-

larity optimization. The granularity at which many non-conventional acceler-

ators are being designed, including area-reusing accelerators and accelerators

resulting from automated hardware-software partitioning, is too fine-grained,

most notably at the basic blocks or loop granularity in the best case.

In this thesis, we propose early-stage solutions for designing non-conventional ac-

celerators that address the suboptimality problems in early-stage system partitioning

and increase the application size/number of applications that can be accelerated per

chip. First, with AccelMerger, we address the EDSE with area reuse in mind to pro-

duce highly eﬀicient accelerators. We use code merging techniques prior to high-level

synthesis to achieve circuitry reuse, and we select profitable merged circuitry not just

in terms of its PPA tradeoffs but also in terms of the data communication require-

ments. Second, we analyze the potential for creating multi-application accelerators

by merging application regions and then synthesizing those merged regions to cre-

ate area and energy-eﬀicient accelerators. We build Guac, a tool relying on sequence

alignment compiler transformations to achieve these PPA improvements inter- and

intra-application while analyzing the impact of statistical PPA models in sequence

alignment techniques. Third, we analyze the limitations in early-stage design space

exploration regarding optimality and error, starting from non-optimized application

implementation. We developed Accura-EDSE, a tool that accurately performs early-

stage design space exploration.

### 1.2 Background

The 90s and the emergence of high-level synthesis. In the 90s, high-level synthesis re-

search emerged to cope with the increasing complexity of hardware accelerator de-

sign17,18,35. In the same way that compilers elevated the level of abstraction from

CPU assembly language, designing hardware accelerators, described with register-

transfer level (RTL) code, could be simplified starting from a high-level language, too.

Another motivation for HLS in the 90s was using digital signal processors (DSPs),

which could accelerate at a good performance per watt floating point operation. HLS

progressed alongside single-core CPU architectural improvements during that decade.

Surprisingly, the typical HLS stages of allocation, scheduling, and binding have re-

mained the same over the decades, with progress focused on supporting different ar-

chitectures and high-level languages. Recently, HLS tools have progressed to cover

high-level representations of code with more parallelism and data locality information

by focusing on a particular domain such as ML77,36 while still supporting applications

written in general-purpose languages like C/C++.

In the 2000s, fine-grained resource sharing and instruction set extensions. In the

2000-2010 period, single-core performance reached its peak, and multi-cores were

chosen as a way to continue extracting performance from the increasing number of

transistors per unit of area. Cores were also becoming more complex by adding fine-

4


<!-- Page 20 -->


grained accelerators in addition to aggressively deep pipelines. This materialized in

the Instruction Set Extension (ISE) literature39,4,69,66,49,10,45, which was looking for

more complex patterns in programs, namely data-flow graphs (DFGs). In the 90s, the

patterns searched were just a few instructions so the DSPs could be leveraged effec-

tively at the right granularity. The research in ISE started using more sophisticated

techniques to match longer strings of instructions. This ISE research literature con-

tinued to be important in the 2010s research, which focused on applications64,33,57.

However, to our knowledge, tightly coupled fine-grained accelerators were not adopted

commercially for CPUs, at least not the kind created via automatic code/circuit

matching methodology. The reason ISE with fine-grained merged accelerators was not

implemented commercially is beyond the scope of this dissertation. Still, we think the

cause was the RISC criticism of complex instructions as well as the already diﬀicult

task of verification and validation of CPUs.

The 2010s, the ML boom, and domain-specific fine-grained ISE. In the early 2010s,

Machine Learning saw a lot of success with the introduction of the ImageNet dataset

and AlexNet convolutional neural network, as well as in the language domain with

Seq2Seq. The computer architecture community soon started manually designing ac-

celerators for ML9,30. EDSE, neither for partitioning nor for merging, was being used

yet, so the designer had to rely on their intuition as to which patterns were worth ac-

celerating across multiple applications and what the right granularity was at which

to create those accelerators. These were loosely coupled coarse-grained accelerators

connected to the CPU via AXI-style interconnect. This early information that accel-

erators would be more favorably designed in a loosely coupled fashion was not imme-

diately leveraged in the design automation research. This led to the continued push

for ISE extensions in the early 2010s Conservation Cores (CCORES)67 and Quasi-

5


<!-- Page 21 -->


Specific Cores (QSCORES)68 which showed the improved energy eﬀiciency of fine-

grained merged accelerators tightly coupled with CPUs. Another major limitation of

these tools was the language coverage, as they were designed for functions with aﬀine

behavior, mostly mathematical functions that could be expressed with a few loops

and were easy to analyze for patterns. Those late-stage DSE tools could only benefit

from computational pattern reuse post-hardware-software partitioning.

Late 2010s, early 2020s, domain-specific accelerators, and ML-assisted DSE. In the

late 2010s and early 2020s, inspired by how accelerators were designed in a loosely-

coupled fashion led to early-stage system design tools26,80,79,78 as well as tools that

detected merging opportunities at coarser granularities37, though in the latter case

inheriting language limitations similar to the ones in late-stage merging tools such as

QSCORES. Developing coarse-grained merging at the level of the C/C++/Abstract-

Syntax-Tree level had the limitation that each statement or instruction can be ar-

bitrarily complex, whereas, in the IR, each instruction is expressed in a short pre-

determined format very amenable for optimizations like function merging. This is an

important reason why most optimizations are implemented at the IR level), being

limited to small kernels and without analysis of the impact of models either in the

selection or the merging problem. A significant development was the emergence of

Post-Moore’s law area-constrained systems rely on accelerators to deliver performance

enhancements. Coarse-grained accelerators can offer substantial domain acceleration,

2.1 Motivation

As CMOS scaling slows, the increase in micro-circuitry per unit area, deciding which

code regions to accelerate becomes harder. However, the demand for improved per-

formance is exacerbated by novel domains such as AR/VR, Robotics, and Machine

Learning that require more agile and eﬀicient design methodologies. The traditional

approach in accelerating novel applications is to manually profile them and decide in

an ad-hoc manner what code regions should be mapped onto hardware. These man-

ual approaches are ad-hoc since they either directly map specific functions or loops

15


<!-- Page 31 -->


onto hardware at a fixed granularity60 and/or informally identify a simple pattern oc-

curring across different functions and create an accelerator for that (e.g.9,30). Code

patterns can be as simple as repeated sequences of multiply-add operations to com-

plex control flow graphs (CFGs) and data flow graphs (DFGs) representing a function

(CDFG) or a function call graph (nested-CDFG). In the case of manual accelerator

design, patterns are only exploited at fine basic-block/DFG-level granularities, based

on the architect’s domain intuition.

To overcome some of these manual aspects of accelerator design, Early-Stage De-

sign Space Exploration (Early-DSE)80,79,26 has emerged as a profiling methodology

able to discover new SoC architectures adjusted to the application’s characteristics.

Furthermore, Early-DSE informs the SoC designer without having to manually trans-

form the most executed application functions into a synthesizable format, i.e. accept-

able by HLS Tools7,44,73,6, an extremely error-prone and time-consuming process.

However, Early-DSE comes unprepared to exploit variable CDFG granularities and

much less to reason about architectures that reuse CDFG logic.

Merging small/fine-grained DFGs68,64,39,10 have been implemented using a graph-

isomorphism approach, at HLS time, therefore missing an opportunity to think about

the whole system in terms of reusing CDFG patterns. These approaches have received

limited adoption in RTL synthesis tools44 7, most likely because graph-isomorphism

is NP-Hard and not very scalable. Additionally, at fine granularities, the benefits of

calling an accelerator are greatly diminished by the cost of updating and reading from

a register file (RF). Similarly, fine-grained merged accelerators tend to be tightly cou-

pled with the general purpose core, for example via the cache memory system. In the

HLS context, RF-less, coarse-grained accelerators have had the most success since rich

CDFGs are mapped to hardware via datapaths handled via control logic. There is no

### 2.7 Discussion

Early-stage accelerator design through function merging, based on the optimized se-

lection of merged and non-merged, hardware-mapped functions and loops, opens an

exciting research space that promises to benefit performance and area/latency trade-

offs. AccelMerger can enable lower, system-level data communication, with a focus on

interconnect latency. It allows designers to explore accelerators of varying granulari-

ties without deep application knowledge, as the choice of accelerators is not fixed by

the structure of an application’s source code. Experimental results show up to 16.7×

performance improvement over software-only implementations, and 1.91× on average

over state-of-the-art HW/SW partitioning tools. In future work, we plan to extend

AccelMerger’s SoC-level communication analysis, apply it for cross-application merges

and add power models to its repertoire.

In the next chapter, we will explore the potential of function merging to improve

energy savings. We will also study the impact of different function merging design

choices, such as the IR representation (SSA or not), local vs. global merging tradeoffs,

alignment, and post-code-generation models.

Designing accelerators for resource- and power-constrained applications is a daunting

task. High-level Synthesis (HLS) addresses these constraints through resource sharing,

an optimization at the HLS binding stage that maps multiple operations to the same

functional unit.

60


<!-- Page 76 -->


However, resource sharing is often limited to reusing instructions within a basic

block. Instead of searching globally for the best control and dataflow graphs (CDFGs)

to combine, it is constrained by existing instruction mappings and schedules.

Coarse-grained function merging (CGFM) at the intermediate representation (IR)

level can reuse control and dataflow patterns without dealing with the post-scheduling

complexity of mapping operations onto functional units, wires, and registers. The

merged functions produced by CGFM can be translated to RTL by HLS, yielding

Coarse Grained Merged Accelerators (CGMAs). CGMAs are especially profitable

across applications with similar data- and control-flow patterns. Prior work has used

CGFM to generate CGMAs without regard for which CGFM algorithms best opti-

mize area, power, and energy costs.

We propose , an energy-aware and SSA-based (static single assignment) CGMA

generation methodology. implements a novel ensemble of cost models for eﬀicient

CGMA generation. We also show that CGFM algorithms using SSA form to merge

control- and dataflow graphs outperform prior non-SSA CGFM designs. We demon-

strate significant area, power, and energy savings with respect to the state of the art.

In particular, more than doubles energy savings with respect to the closest related

work while using a strong resource-sharing baseline.

3.1 Motivation

Manual accelerator designs attempt to reuse fine-grained control and dataflow ap-

plication patterns through the design of processing elements (PEs). Such manual

implementations can be found in cutting-edge domains such as deep learning and

robotics30,63,60. These multi-purpose accelerators greatly benefit from area and power

61


<!-- Page 77 -->


optimizations due to the large number of impacted applications. On the other hand,

automated HLS-level resource sharing28,4 uses analytical models that assume a spe-

cific cost per operation. These works do not study the models’ impact on the acceler-

ator design’s quality. The lack of model studies is due to the multi-layered nature of

the HLS stages, including allocation, scheduling, and binding. Instruction cost mod-

els, when trained statistically, cannot minimize an objective function representing

HLS allocation, scheduling, and binding to understand functional unit reuse prof-

itability. Instead, a cost model mapping IR-level instruction characteristics to accel-

erator characteristics, e.g., power, performance, and area, is built and used as part of

the HLS process when deciding which functional units to reuse. In the related work,

not much attention has been paid to the mismatch between modeling instructions and

modeling functional units. Models are rarely discussed at all in the context of eﬀicient

HLS resource sharing.

Resource sharing works at fine granularity, finding functional units without struc-

tural conflicts that inhibit reuse. Conflict-free reused chains of functional units accel-

erate small, semantically equivalent dataflow graphs scheduled for different cycles. In

our experiments with state-of-the-art HLS and physical design tools, we find that this

kind of resource sharing reduces energy consumption by 45.79% with respect to accel-

erators not benefiting from resource sharing. (See Section 3.3.2 and Section 3.6.2)

Resource sharing, however, has a myopic view of what needs to be reused post-

scheduling. It looks at accelerator reuse not from the perspective of dataflow, control

flow, or input/output reuse but from a functional unit and structural conflict per-

spective. Some accelerator merging tools have sought to address this problem. Re-

confAST37 produces merged accelerators at the loop level in a front-end compiler

(clang), but at such a high level, optimization support is limited. AccelMerger5 lever-

62


<!-- Page 78 -->


ages the function merging by sequence alignment (FMSA) algorithm developed in

the related work52. AccelMerger works at LLVM’s intermediate representation (IR)

level to provide coarse-grained function merging (CGFM), which merges functions

and their call graphs. AccelMerger takes advantage of LLVM’s rich framework for

target-independent interprocedural optimization rather than working on the abstract

syntax tree.

These accelerator merging tools introduce a new way of designing accelerators that

are more programmable than monolithic accelerators in that they can accelerate more

than one top-level function or application. We call them CGMA, standing for coarse-

grained merged accelerators. They are less programmable than finer-grained recon-

figurable architectures, which spend significant area for functional unit (FU) and in-

terconnect programmability. Finer-grained reconfigurable architectures suffer from

significant communication overheads since they accelerate small control and dataflow

patterns. A CGMA can approach the performance of the original monolithic acceler-

ators from which it derives while consuming only a fraction of their total energy and

area. CGFM can produce energy and area savings only for accelerators representing

similar CDFGs. This similarity requirement puts pressure on the CGFM technique to

better understand the impact of local merging decisions on end-to-end energy savings.

In this work, we develop CGFM models aimed at eﬀicient CGMA design, and we

identify the best CGFM algorithms for high CGMA energy savings. We choose en-

ergy savings as a proxy for co-optimizing power, performance, and area. An HLS tool

can produce a monolithic accelerator starting from a function’s high-level or IR-level

representation. After selecting and merging a pair of related functions, we use HLS to

produce a merged accelerator for the pair.

Few prior works can merge at such coarse granularities. To the best of our knowl-

Prior work on CGMA does not analyze the potential of merging models to generate

### 3.3 Background

3.3.1 High Level Synthesis

High Level Synthesis translates high-level code like C/C++ to Verilog or VHDL. Its

stages typically include Allocation, Scheduling, Binding and RTL generation18,36,22.

We focus on the first three of these since the last stage just translates from the HLS

internal representation of functional units and registers to RTL.

Allocation uses device operation modeling to produce an initial estimate of the area

required by an accelerator, especially in terms of functional units.

Scheduling is the phase in which the HLS tool distributes operations across cycles,

taking into account their dependencies. Dependent instructions are chained together

within the same cycle if they do not violate a target cycle time. In this step the Con-

trol Logic of the accelerator is generated, typically as a finite state machine. Neither

allocation nor scheduling has a concept of functional units on which operations will be

scheduled.

Binding constitutes the mapping of operations onto functional units. In this step,

HLS executes the resource sharing optimization by mapping multiple operations onto

the same functional unit if they are not executed in the same cycle. If the dataflow

style of the reused functional unit chain is identical to a previously bound operation

chain, no multiplexing is needed. However, input and output operands usually need

to be routed differently, and expensive multiplexers need to be used. For this reason,

only long latency instructions or chains thereof are reused.

3.3.4 Function Merging by Sequence Alignment

FMSA overview. FMSA52 was the first CGFM algorithm able to merge arbitrary

non-identical pairs of functions introduced with the goal of reducing code size. It was

later used in the context of high level synthesis5 for area reduction (AccelMerger).

We now focus on the FMSA flow at the LLVM IR level. The algorithm consists of

three major stages: choosing which functions to merge, producing the merged func-

tion, and estimating the merging profitability.

Function Pairing. In this chapter, we perform merging across multiple applica-

tions and we merge all pairs of functions in the input applications since some pairings

might be profitable only for some techniques and not for others. This pairing is differ-

ent than in the previous chapter since the goal is to strictly evaluate the improvement

in the merging techniques, both for accelerators that were already profitable as well as

those that were not (and will potentially become profitable).

Function Linearization. For a given pair of functions, merging them requires iden-

73


<!-- Page 89 -->


tifying similar code segments in the two functions that can profitably be merged. To

this end, FMSA52 first linearizes the input functions, representing the CFG as a se-

quence of instructions.

Alignment. Then the Needleman-Wunsch (NW) sequence alignment algorithm

identifies regions of similarity between the two functions. The alignment algorithm

is applied to the linearized sequences of the whole input functions. The NW algo-

rithm allows weighting each operation. In this work, our alignment models provide

the NW weighting of instructions. Finally, the resulting alignment is used to generate

the merged function.

Code Generation. During code generation, the list of parameters from both func-

tions is also merged using a greedy algorithm that tries to merge as many parameters

as possible. Parameters of the same type are shared between the functions, without

necessarily keeping their original order. The merged list of parameters also includes

an extra function identifier. All the calling sites for the input functions are also mod-

ified to point to the newly merged functions with the right parameter order and origi-

nal function identifier.

New Basic Blocks for Contiguous Aligned and Unaligned Instructions. Once the

function definition has been created, the control-flow graph of the merged function

is produced by traversing both the input functions and the aligned sequence. The

merged control-flow graph uses the function identifier for control flow divergence

where the two functions differ, but converges to the same basic block where they

are similar. Operand selection is also introduced where two merged instructions have

different operands. Finally, FMSA applies an SSA reconstruction algorithm on the

merged function.

non-linear models, able to extract more information about accelerator power and area

characteristics by analyzing function-level characteristics such as number of instruc-

register demotion and increases the chances of generating profitable merged functions.

excluding them from function alignment since in most cases FMSA would miss-align

the equivalent alloca, store, and load operations. This leads in practice to more saved

and store instructions corresponding to the phi instructions correctly against other

3.4.1 CGFM for accelerator energy eﬀiciency

Alignment and post-code-generation energy model. The main shortcoming in the

related work is that CGFM techniques do not merge for energy savings. There are

two possible approaches to making CGFM energy-savings-aware. One way is by using

alignment models. Algorithms like Needleman-Wunsch (NW) can align sequences

with a linear model, attributing a cost to each instruction type. The result is that

NW finds the alignment with the lowest cost due to the algorithm’s optimality guarantees.

The second possible energy model considered in this chapter is post-code-generation.

It is applied on the resulting CDFG after aligning two functions. Post-code-generation

models evaluate the potential energy savings directly using the features of the merged

function instead of some abstract representation of the function (e.g., the sequences

used in the sequence alignment algorithm).

We use alignment-time merging to create multiple versions of a merged function,

while taking account of the accelerator back end. Then we apply a code-generation-time

statistical model based on random forests to select the accelerator version most likely

The per-slice logic is under-utilized when an application is memory-, compute- or

control-intense. Still, a good balance of resource usage allows HLS to map more operations

### 3.7 Related Work

Most coarse grained merging for accelerator design is occurring in the context of

manual code analysis and acceleration60,9,30,63. In this work, we improve automated

96


<!-- Page 112 -->


coarse-grained merging to further motivate the use of coarse-grained accelerator merging.

The main related works in coarse-grained accelerator merging are AccelMerger5

and ReconfAST37. They rely on analytical models to provide merging information

early in accelerator design, while in this chapter we focus on a highly accurate C/LLVM-to-bitstream

approach. ReconfAST implements the merging optimization in the C-front-end layer

of clang (pre-LLVM), which makes it specific to a single high-level language, and

less likely to benefit from mainstream compiler optimization research. Also, IRs are

simpler and more amenable to optimizations like CGFM than high-level languages.

For example, control flow in the IR is handled with branch and phi instructions,

whereas at a high-level there are many control-related constructs, such as while, for,

do while, if and switch statements.

There is a large body of work on resource sharing that have shaped the area and

power optimizations implemented in HLS and physical design tools4,68,64,67,28,39,10.

Even though some related works discuss PPA estimation14,13,81,5,76,23 these models

are rarely used for compiler optimization and not with the goal of interprocedural

optimization aimed at CGMA generation. Cycle-accurate accelerator simulation literature

has used linear operation-level optimizations but coarse grained accelerator merging

is out of the scope of these works53,54. CGFM-based CGMA accelerator works37,5 by

contrast contain no contributions on models either at alignment time nor at post-code-generation

time.

FMSA, HyFM and SalSSA52,51,50 are LLVM compilation transformations aimed

code reduction. These techniques use the CPU ISA (linear) model for code size out of

the box to guide the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm in finding an optimal alignment.

Since LLVM lacks FPGA cost models, we implement our own cost models and replace

candidate selection. Since HLS stages are much more complicated than mapping IR

4.1 Motivation

Late DSE is a consolidated field in design automation with tools like gem5-Aladdin55

and gem5-SALAM53 used to simulate SoCs with CPUs and accelerators. These tools

rely on a tedious and error-prone process to partition the application for CPU and

accelerator execution. They also rely on the hardware designer to convert code to

a format with simple data structures such as arrays and no hardware side effects.

Late-DSE requires many iterations implementing data communication between the

100


<!-- Page 116 -->


CPU and accelerator as well as optimizing the hardware-related code, all in a post-partitioning

stage of SoC design.

Deciding how to partition code, however, especially in the case of complex applications,

is still an open problem. Tools like RegionSeeker80, Trireme78, and AccelSeeker79

have pioneered an approach to the application partitioning problem under the name

of Early-Stage Design Space Exploration (EDSE). EDSE promises to provide hardware-software

partitioning feedback starting from source code and high-level architectural constraints.

One major flaw inherited by EDSE from Late-DSE is a reliance on expert analytical

models to produce early-stage estimates for hardware latency and area. These expert

models estimate the costs of instructions and are the basis for making coarser granularity

estimates for basic blocks, regions, functions, and function hierarchies. Those estimated

costs are hardcoded in the source code of the EDSE and Late-DSE tools. In the case

of Late-DSE, since simulation tools emulate many of the stages of High-Level-Synthesis

(HLS) flows, they manage to achieve remarkable accuracy on both latency and area.

These stages include loop pipelining, phi-node and memory instruction removal, buffering,

and fusion. These Late-DSE steps are possible when the source code is synthesizable

and its hardware and software partitions have been chosen. EDSE, however, must

achieve reasonable accuracy without being able to reproduce in great detail the HLS

steps. It is not clear from the related work whether building an EDSE that extrapolates

to new applications is possible, with what accuracy, and what are the optimality

limitations of the EDSE solutions.

Expert models used in EDSE tools (and also in Late-DSE tools) tend to have these

Underfitting

4.3 Accura-EDSE, our proposed EDSE design

In our approach termed Accura-EDSE, we address the interaction between optimization

(MILP-based) and inaccuracies inherent to the inputs of the EDSE problem.

*Figure 4.2 shows how Accura-EDSE updates the flow of Figure 4.1. A statistical*

model replaces Part A. Part B eliminates code transformations and critical path

Instead, Accura-EDSE applies statistical models to static and dynamic instruction

4.3.1 Addressing underfitting, overfitting and linearity problems in expert mod-

Accelerator latency. To avoid underfitting, we predict the hardware latency HW(f) =

CALLS(f) ∗HWone_call(f) of each function f. We use dynamic instruction counts for one

call of f to build a model for HWone_call(f). CALLS(f) is available in the application

dynamic instrumentation during the early stages of design. In our experiments, just

predicting HWone_call(f), while using the true value of CALLS(f), dramatically increases

the accuracy of HW(f) estimates. In fact, we observe that even linear latency models

deliver close to 97.3% accuracy for HW(f) when we focus on predicting HWone_call(f)

and leverage the true CALLS(f) information. The most sophisticated models that

try to predict HW(f) struggle to achieve high accuracy, even for CPU latency34, but

especially for accelerator latency71,70,58,16.

Area Estimates. For predicting AREA(f), we noticed that the linearity problem is

important and that linear models such as linear regression and Lasso tend to lead to

EDSE inaccuracy. To address these problems, we use a model that is able to exploit

non-linearities in area prediction, namely random forests. In Section 4.5.3, we show a

marked increase in solution optimality (area and latency improvements due to optimal

selection) as well as highly accurate reports to the EDSE tool user. As discussed in

Section 4.5.1, non-linear models also mitigate area budget violations that occur in

tools that rely on linear models. Experiments with other non-linear models, such

as the Multilayer-Perceptron (MLP), did not yield increased accuracy on this data.

For HWone_call(f), we use hierarchical dynamic instruction counts for one call of f

### 4.6 Related Work

A goal of EDSE tools is to select the most feasible functions for acceleration to maximize

performance subject to resource constraints such as area and communication constraints.

EDSE selection can be performed using MILP, or other design space exploration

techniques including semi-brute-force algorithms such as independent-set detection79,80

118


<!-- Page 134 -->


or exhaustive design space search81. These EDSE non-MILP79,80 and other MILP-based

related works5,41,81 are focused on software-hardware partitioning, overlooking the

interaction between model accuracy and overall solution optimality and accuracy.

In this work, we compare against79 because of the granularity, system modeling and

degree to which it addresses the EDSE problem (see AccelSeeker discussion in Section 4.2).

By contrast, the focus of late-stage DSE tools55,53 is on detailed point solutions,

which can only be slowly evaluated. Another class of Late-DSE tools is represented

by FARSI3 and Platform Architect61. They are late-stage DSE, even in their agile

execution models, because they rely on existing code partitioning and expert analysis

of each partition to perform system-level DSE. There are tools that trade-off some

EDSE flexibility for closer-to-late-DSE accuracy, behaving more like Late-DSE. Examples

include41 and78, but they require porting the application to a new (often domain

specific) language.

### 4.7 Discussion

In this chapter, we focused on the EDSE accelerator selection problem for systems

with CPU and accelerators. We isolated the effect of expert linear models that train

and test on the same applications, a methodology consistently applied both in the

space of EDSE and Late-DSE. We propose an alternative design with Accura-EDSE,

which has an error as low as 2.6% and 6.6% for latency and area, respectively, while

making EDSE problems up to 83.3× larger than related work feasible in the time

frame of a few minutes.

Early-stage non-conventional accelerator discovery through flexible hardware/software

partitioning and merging was mostly believed to be relevant for smaller sub-problems

in early-stage design-space exploration. Some examples are 1) improving the feedback

a designer can get with tools better than those used for software profiling and 2)
